samples.text:
The three pie charts shows the different sources which was used to produce electricity in one country in 2000, 2012 and 2024.

In 2000 coal was the main source, it produced 52% of electricity. Gas was 20% and nuclear was 18%. Hydro was 8% and wind and solar were only 2%, which is very small.

In 2012 coal decreased to 38% but it was still the biggest source. Gas increased to 28% and wind and solar also increased to 9%. Nuclear was nearly the same with 17% and hydro did not change at all, it stayed at 8%.

In 2024 there was a big change. Wind and solar became the largest source with 34%, and gas was second with 30%. Coal dropped a lot to only 12%. Nuclear fell a little to 15% and hydro was 9%.

Overall, the country used less coal and much more wind and solar energy over the period, and gas also become more important, but nuclear and hydro stayed around the same.
samples.why: All three charts covered with accurate figures · overview present but basic and placed last · paragraph-by-year structure is mechanical · limited range of linking and vocabulary · several agreement, tense and punctuation errors.

samples.text:
The pie charts illustrate how electricity was generated in one country in 2000, 2012 and 2024.

Overall, there was a dramatic shift away from coal towards wind and solar power over the period. Gas also became increasingly important, whereas nuclear and hydro power remained relatively stable.

In 2000, coal was by far the most important source, generating more than half of the country's electricity (52%). Gas and nuclear power accounted for 20% and 18% respectively, while hydro contributed 8%. Wind and solar were almost insignificant at this time, producing only 2%.

By 2012, the share of coal had fallen to 38%, although it was still the leading source. Meanwhile, gas rose to 28% and wind and solar grew to 9%. In 2024, however, the situation had changed completely. Wind and solar had become the largest source, at 34%, which was seventeen times its share in 2000. Gas continued to rise slightly to 30%, whereas coal dropped sharply to just 12%. Over the whole period, nuclear power declined only marginally, from 18% to 15%, and hydro stayed at around 8–9%.
samples.why: Clear overview of the main trends · key changes across three charts well highlighted · accurate figures with a valid derived comparison · logical progression and varied linking · mostly error-free sentences.

samples.text:
The charts compare the contribution of five energy sources to electricity generation in one country at three points between 2000 and 2024.

Over the period, the country's electricity mix was transformed: coal, initially the dominant source, was largely displaced by wind and solar power, with gas also expanding its share. Nuclear and hydroelectric generation, by contrast, remained fairly constant.

In 2000, coal supplied just over half of all electricity (52%), with gas (20%) and nuclear (18%) making up most of the remainder. Hydro accounted for 8%, and wind and solar generated a negligible 2%.

The following twelve years saw the beginning of a shift. Coal's share contracted to 38%, while gas climbed to 28% and wind and solar more than quadrupled to 9%. This trend accelerated markedly after 2012, so that by 2024 wind and solar had become the largest source, providing 34% of electricity, whereas coal had plummeted to only 12%, a fall of 40 percentage points since 2000. Gas edged up further to 30%, making it the second most important source. Throughout the period, nuclear power declined only slightly, from 18% to 15%, and hydro remained almost unchanged at 8–9%.
samples.why: Key features skilfully selected across three charts · overview clear and well placed · accurate figures used for purposeful comparison · cohesion managed smoothly · precise vocabulary · wide range of error-free structures.
